57-015.r: Dadabhai Naoroji ('Grand Old Man of India') → first Indian to become a Member of British Parliament (UK House of Commons).
57-015.t: Don't confuse with Surendranath Banerjee or Ras Bihari Bose; only Naoroji sat in the House of Commons.

57-016.r: Surat Session 1907 (President Rash Behari Ghosh) → Congress split into Moderates (Naram Dal) and Extremists (Garam Dal); trigger: 1906 Calcutta resolutions on Swadeshi, Boycott, National Education, Swaraj.
57-016.h: Surat = Split: both start with S.

57-021.r: Early twentieth-century Congress split (Surat, December 1907) began over all three: strategies, objectives and people's participation in the Congress movement.

57-022.r: 1907 session → President Rash Behari Ghosh; Congress split into Moderates and Extremists (both true). 1916 reunion session was presided by Ambikacharan Mazumdar, not S.P. Sinha (false).

57-023.r: Surat split → 1907 (first split of Congress); Extremists side led by Tilak against the Moderates.

57-026.r: Main reason for Surat split 1907 → Extremists' lack of faith in Moderates' capacity to negotiate with the British; Extremists wanted to extend Swadeshi and Boycott.

58-001.r: All India Muslim League → founded 1906 at Dhaka; founder/host Nawab Salimullah; Aga Khan III was a founding member and first President.
58-001.t: Don't confuse founder Nawab Salimullah with first President Aga Khan III or with Sir Syed Ahmad Khan.

58-006.r: Muslim League: founded 1906 at Dhaka; first annual session 1907 at Karachi; 1908 session at Amritsar.
58-006.h: D-K-A order: Dhaka (founded) → Karachi (first session) → Amritsar (next).

58-007.r: Muslim League sessions: 1907 Karachi, 1908 Amritsar, then held erratically; so no option fits (BPSC key accepted 1925, book disagrees).

58-008.r: League refused to accept Congress Muslims, posing as sole representative of Indian Muslims → A correct; R ('only League has this right') wrong.

58-009.r: Muslim League (1906) supported Bengal partition and demanded separate electorates (Aga Khan III), not opposed; Sayyed Ahmad Khan opposed Congress; Barkat Ullah, Obeidullah Sindhi → Provisional Government, Kabul.

58-010.r: Shimla Deputation (1 October 1906), led by Aga Khan III, met Viceroy Lord Minto → pleaded for separate electorate for Muslims.

58-011.r: London branch of All India Muslim League (1908) → President Syed Ameer Ali; League headquarters at Lucknow.

58-012.r: W.W. Hunter, 'The Indian Musalmans' → 'Muslims, if contented and satisfied, would become the greatest bulwark of British power in India'.

59-001.r: 1911 (Delhi Durbar, 12 December) → annulment of 1905 Bengal Partition announced and capital transfer Calcutta to Delhi; Lucknow Pact was not in 1911.

59-002.r: Morley-Minto Reforms = Indian Councils Act, 1909; Lord Minto Viceroy (replaced Curzon, 1905), John Morley Secretary of State for India.

59-003.r: Indian Councils Act 1909 (Morley-Minto) → communal representation: separate electorate, Muslim members elected only by Muslim voters.

59-004.r: Seeds of discord that divided the country → reserved seats and separate electorates for Muslims (Minto-Morley reforms); first treated Muslims as a separate section.

59-005.r: Rajendra Prasad called Lord Minto 'Father of Pakistan' → Minto-Morley reforms of 1909 introduced communal electorates, sowing seeds of partition.
59-005.h: Minto → separate electorates → seeds of Pakistan.

60-001.r: Calcutta was British India's capital until 1911; George V announced shift to Delhi at Delhi Durbar (12 December 1911); shifted 1912 under Lord Hardinge II.

60-003.r: Delhi as capital → announced 1911 (Delhi Durbar, King George V); transfer completed 1912. If both given, book prefers 1912.

60-007.r: Bomb thrown at Viceroy Lord Hardinge II on his State entry into Delhi (23 December) → Delhi-Lahore Conspiracy, 1912, headed by Rash Behari Bose.

60-009.r: Hardinge Bomb (Delhi Conspiracy) Case → death sentence: Awadh Bihari, Master Amir Chand, Balmukund, Basant Biswas; Bhagwati Charan Vohra not involved; Rash Behari Bose fled to Japan.

60-010.r: Bomb thrown at Viceroy Lord Hardinge II in Delhi → Anushilan Samiti (book answer); leader Rash Behari Bose.
60-010.t: Book answer is Anushilan Samiti, not Yugantar.

60-011.r: Delhi Durbar (December 1911) separated Bihar and Orissa from Bengal; Bihar became a separate administrative unit in 1912.

60-012.r: Bihar from Bengal: announced 12 December 1911; Bihar and Orissa province proclaimed 22 March 1912, existed from 1 April 1912; Bihar alone a province in 1936.

61-001.r: December 1916 → Congress and Muslim League both held sessions at Lucknow → Lucknow Pact (Hindu-Muslim unity, composition of legislatures).

61-002.r: Lucknow Session 1916 → President A.C. (Ambika Charan) Majumdar; Lucknow Pact signed between Congress and Muslim League.

61-004.r: Lucknow 1916: Extremists re-entered Congress after 9 years → chief architect Annie Besant (with Tilak); Congress-League agreement credited to B.G. Tilak.

61-006.r: Lucknow Pact 1916 → Congress first accepted separate electorates for Muslims, a decision with long-term implications.

61-008.r: Congress-Muslim League unanimity → 1916-1922 (Lucknow Pact until it dissolved with Non-Cooperation Movement).

61-009.r: Lucknow Session 1916 → President Ambika Charan Majumdar (so 'not President' is wrong); Moderate-Extremist reunion; Gandhi first told of Champaran peasants.
61-009.h: Lucknow 1916 = three events: Pact, Reunion, Champaran.

61-010.r: Lucknow Session 1916 → Raj Kumar Shukla told Gandhi about Champaran peasants' problems.

62-001.r: Home Rule Leagues 1916 → Tilak's (April, HQ Poona) and Annie Besant's (September, HQ Adyar near Madras); book answer for 'first launched': Annie Besant.
62-001.c: Tilak's League came first (April 1916; Besant's in September 1916), but the book answers Besant because she first proposed Home Rule, in The Common Weal (1914).

62-003.r: Annie Besant (theosophist) → Home Rule Movement, popular during First World War; League formed September 1916 at Adyar, Madras; inspired by Irish Home Rule.

62-005.r: H.S. Olcott → Theosophical Society, not Home Rule League; contributors: Tilak, Annie Besant, S. Subramania Iyer. C.R. Das also not associated.

62-007.r: Lucknow Congress Session (December 1916) → Home Rule supporters successfully demonstrated their political strength.

62-008.r: Home Rule Movement began a new phase → it placed a perfect plan of self-government (within British Empire, by constitutional means) before the nation.

62-009.r: Home Rule idea first introduced by Annie Besant (The Commonweal, 2 January 1914); Tilak's League April 1916, Poona; Besant and S. Subramania Iyer's September 1916, Adyar.
62-009.c: The book finds all four statements correct (the two Leagues complemented each other and both continued), so it prints no answer for 'not correct'.

62-011.r: Annie Besant (1847-1933) → proponent of Fabianism (Fabian movement).

62-012.r: Annie Besant → started Home Rule Movement; first woman Congress President (1917, Calcutta); not founder of Theosophical Society (Madame Blavatsky and Henry Olcott).
62-012.t: Besant led the Theosophical Society in India but did not found it.

62-013.r: Annie Besant visited Bihar (Patna) in 1918 → 18 April to strengthen Home Rule League; 25 July to understand Home Rulers' views.

62-014.r: 1920 → All India Home Rule League (Annie Besant, founded September 1916) renamed 'Swarajya Sabha'.

63-001.r: Karamchand (Kaba) Gandhi, Gandhiji's father → Diwan of Porbandar, Rajkot and Wankaner (all three).

63-002.r: Gandhiji studied at Samaldas (Arts) College, Bhavnagar in 1885.

63-003.r: Gandhi in South Africa → newspaper 'Indian Opinion'; Natal Indian Congress (1894); Phoenix Farm at Durban (1904); Tolstoy Farm.

63-006.r: Gandhi → supporter of philosophical anarchism (also linked to Utopian socialism); stressed practical idealism, not mere idealism.

63-007.r: Twin principles of Gandhi's Ram Rajya → Truth and Non-violence.

63-008.r: Gandhi: Ahimsa (non-violence) is the means, Truth is the end → non-violence is a way to attain truth.
63-008.h: Ahimsa = the path; Satya = the destination.

63-009.r: Gandhi described as 'an Individualist among Socialists and a Marxist among Socialists'; linked to philosophical anarchism but accepted a minimal State.

63-010.r: Gandhian Satyagraha → fast is the first step (called 'Fire Arrow'); strike is the last step.
63-010.h: Fast First, Strike at the end.

63-011.r: Satyagraha aims to change the opponent's perception, not to defeat the enemy; its weapon is Ahimsa; no ill feeling towards opponents.

63-012.r: Gandhiji: cruelest form of violence → persistence of poverty.
